big_case_rationale: Decides whether the VPPA's 'consumer' definition sustains the large wave of pixel-tracking class actions against media and retail companies; high industry stakes (Meta, MPA, Chamber amici) but technical statutory subject matter with modest general-public salience.

semantic_claims.proposition: The majority affirms on contextual-textualist grounds: 'goods or services from a video tape service provider' in 18 U.S.C. § 2710(a)(1) means the audiovisual goods or services the provider offers in its statutorily defined capacity — reading the renter/purchaser/subscriber triad in parallel with § 2710(a)(4)'s 'rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audio visual materials' and reinforcing that reading with § 2710(a)(3)'s limitation of personally identifiable information to 'specific video materials or services' — so a subscriber to a free online newsletter is not a 'consumer.' It adopts the Sixth and D.C. Circuits' construction and rejects petitioner's meaningful-variation and 'any'-based plain-meaning argument as reading the unmodified phrase 'goods or services' shorn of its prepositional and structural context.

The majority's stated ground is categorical rather than fact-bound: it announces a general construction of 'consumer' under which VPPA protection requires renting, purchasing, or subscribing to audiovisual goods or services, resolving the circuit split with a rule that forecloses newsletter-subscription and other non-audiovisual-subscription VPPA suits across the board, not a narrow holding limited to Salazar or to 247Sports' newsletter; the main question it leaves open is the one assumed below — whether Paramount qualifies as a 'video tape service provider' at all.
